item.title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
item.dc:creator: Stefan Rahmstorf, Levke Caesar
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: tipping point, Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, climate change, global warming
arXiv:2611.23429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45{\deg}N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

item.title: Proglacial lakes substantially modulate the surface mass balance of deglacial ice sheets
item.dc:creator: Lianne Sijbrandij, Uta Krebs-Kanzow, Paul Gierz, Gregor Knorr, Lu Niu, Shan Xu, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, surface mass balance, surface melt
Towards the end of the last ice age large proglacial lakes formed at the margins of the retreating ice sheets, potentially staying cold due to the influence of melting ice. Modeling shows these lakes lowered summer air temperatures, increased snowfall, and in total reduced surface melt by 18 %–27 % for nearby ice sheets. If lakes stayed below 4 °C, melt dropped by 23 %–35 %, providing a substantial negative feedback for retreating of ice sheets.

item.title: Long‐Term Surface Meltwater Variability and Surface Fracture Patterns on the Amery Ice Shelf
item.dc:creator: Tingting Zhu, Yi Wang, Yu Zhang, Xiangbin Cui
item.category: New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics
item.description:
New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics — matched: ice shelf, Antarctic, meltwater
Antarctic ice shelves buttress grounded ice, but surface meltwater can promote fracture opening when it enters pre‐existing crevasses. Although meltwater variability, water depth and fracture features have been examined separately on the Amery Ice Shelf, their spatial correspondence has received less attention. We integrated January meltwater maps for 2005–2026 with depth and volume estimates for melt seasons ending in 2014–2026 within a common spatial framework. Fracture inputs comprised published creavasse extraction maps for 2009 and 2014 and a Landsat‐derived map for 2025. Multi‐year melt water and creavess coupling indices described relative spatial co‐location. Seasonal indices combined water proximity, local fracture context and retrieved depth. Estimated seasonal volume peaked at 0.76 km 3 in 2017 and 0.75 km 3 in 2019. The 2025 volume was 0.44 km 3 , with generally smaller retrieved depths than in 2014 and 2017. January mapped meltwater area ranged from 26.2 km 2 in 2021 to 1178.1 km 2 in 2005 and reached 1058.4 km 2 in 2025. Recurrently mapped meltwater was concentrated in western and southwestern sectors and along central flow‐aligned zones. The fracture maps showed broadly similar regional zones. The 2014 and 2025 seasonal indices had higher relative values in the western and southwestern sectors. The multi‐year recurrence–fracture comparison showed a similar regional concentration. Adding maximum retrieved depth from seasons ending in 2014–2025 further localised the highest relative multi‐year index values in these sectors. The southeastern sector contained extensive mapped fractures with comparatively limited hydrological co‐location. These results identify regional concentrations of recurrently mapped meltwater, greater retrieved depth and mapped fractures.

item.title: Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
item.dc:creator: Friso de Graaf, David Thornalley, David J. Wilson, Zarina Hewett, Yair Rosenthal, Stella C. Woodard, … (+1)
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, interglacial, Pliocene
Abstract Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (ε Nd ) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability.

item.title: Coupled Ocean–Atmosphere Processes Associated with Realistically Sized Weddell Sea Polynyas in CMIP6 Models
item.dc:creator: Holly Ayres, David Ferreira, Carmen H. M. Wong, Joakim Kjellsson, Malin Ödalen
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: Southern Ocean, sea level, model intercomparison, CMIP
Abstract The mechanisms of the Weddell Sea Polynya have been frequently discussed in the literature since the first and largest observed opening in the 1970s, with smaller Maud Rise Polynyas opening in more recent years. Here we assess both the oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and response associated with polynya events, using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Pre-industrial Control models. Here, we focus on polynyas with realistic size and location (i.e., comparable to the 1970s events). Only two models in the CMIP6 suite produce such realistic polynyas in large numbers, ACCESS-ESM1.5 and MPI-ESM1-2-HR. Their oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and atmospheric response are explored using a composite analysis. We find that weakened stratification sets the oceanic preconditioning, while the onset of polynya years is associated with the occurrence of large-scale atmospheric internal variability, including a ZW3-like pressure and wind pattern. Both modes emerge from internal atmospheric variability, suggesting that the first occurrence in a series of polynya years is stochastic in nature. Once the polynya opens, two-way air-sea feedbacks deepen the sea level pressure anomalies, enabling multi-year polynya events. Through this, the stratification returns to a base level, the ocean state recharges, and the cycle repeats. These results advance understanding of Weddell Sea Polynya formation and highlight the importance of coupled ocean–atmosphere feedbacks in the Southern Ocean.

item.title: Using a Gaussian process emulator to approximate short-term climate response patterns to greenhouse gas and aerosol forcings
item.dc:creator: Laura A. Mansfield, Peer J. Nowack, Edmund M. Ryan, Oliver Wild, Apostolos Voulgarakis
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: greenhouse gas, emulator, machine learning
We present a fast machine learning emulator that predicts how Earth's surface temperature reacts within the first five years to changes in greenhouse gases and aerosol pollutants. It is trained on carefully designed simulations from a complex climate model, but can be run much faster. Our emulator can be used to show where the climate is most sensitive to different emissions and can help explore many possible future paths, making it easier to assess the climate effects of policy choices.

item.title: An antiplane shear model for evaluating shear-margin stability (Ortholine v1.0)
item.dc:creator: Jenny Suckale, Cooper W. Elsworth, Neelanjan Akuli
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: ice stream, glacier, Antarctic, sea level, sea-level rise
The widths of glaciers and ice streams can change over time, which strongly affects how much ice is lost to the ocean. Many existing models of sea-level rise neglect these width changes, but they are commonly observed and important. This paper presents a new, simple model that helps identify which physical factors govern width changes at different field sites. The model is explained step by step and tested using an Antarctic ice stream as an example.

item.title: Post-depositional geochemical transformations of aerosol impurities in EPICA Dome C ice core: dissolution, mineral neoformation, and immobilization revealed by CFA-sp-ICP-TOFMS
item.dc:creator: Geunwoo Lee, Tobias Erhardt, Piers Larkman, Chantal Zeppenfeld, Sarah Jackson, Jochen Schmitt, … (+8)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Antarctic, ice core
Deep ice cores preserve records of past climate, but chemical reactions inside the ice can blur these signals over time. To find out how, we studied millions of dust particles in a deep Antarctic ice core. We found that, over long timescales, dust dissolves and reforms into new minerals within tiny pockets of liquid, trapping chemical elements. Warm temperatures speed up this process. Accounting for it helps scientists interpret ancient climate records from deep ice more reliably.

item.title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model
item.dc:creator: Eliot J. Kim, Eric J. Mei, Peter D. Ivatt, Lee T. Murray, Alexander J. Turner
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation
arXiv:2611.24020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.

item.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
item.dc:creator: Ralf Greve, Bj\"orn Grieger, Oliver J. Stenzel
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: polar, insolation, transient simulation, parameterization
arXiv:2611.23643v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

item.title: Global Holocene Stalagmite Growth Rates and Their Climatic Associations
item.dc:creator: Hao Tan, Jiaxin He, Chang Shu, Haiyan Fang, Guoliang Lei
item.description:
Quaternary — matched: paleoclimate, Holocene
Stalagmite growth rates record cave carbonate deposition and environmental change, but their climatic associations remain insufficiently tested at the global Holocene scale. We compiled 218 stalagmites from 139 caves in SISALv3, calculated mean Holocene growth rates, and matched their growth intervals to gridded paleoclimate variables. Spearman rank correlations, partial least-squares regression, and XGBoost classification were used to assess climatic associations. Growth rates ranged from 0.003 to 1.75 mm yr−1, with 75% of samples below 0.1248 mm yr−1. Annual precipitation showed a weak positive correlation with growth rate (ρ = 0.161), whereas wettest-quarter precipitation, precipitation seasonality, precipitation concentration, and wet-season precipitation ratio showed stronger correlations with growth rate (ρ = 0.288–0.306). Temperature associations were more consistent: mean annual, coldest-quarter, and wettest-quarter temperatures were positively correlated with growth rate (ρ = 0.356–0.422), while temperature seasonality was negatively correlated (ρ = −0.328). An XGBoost model using five climate variables achieved 69.32% accuracy in two-fold cross-validation. These results indicate that climate captures part of the spatial variability in stalagmite growth. Growth rates reflect the combined effects of effective recharge, thermal conditions, karst hydrology, and cave depositional environments, providing a global reference for interpreting Holocene stalagmite records.

item.title: Warming Trends on the Hurd Peninsula of Livingston Island, Antarctica, Between 2000 and 2024, and Improvements in the Estimation of Air Temperature Using C6.1 MODIS LST Data
item.dc:creator: Carmen Recondo González, Alejandro Corbea-Pérez, María del Rosario González-Moradas, Enrique Pendás-Recondo, Miguel Ángel de Pablo, Cristina Allende-Prieto
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: Antarctic, Antarctica, polar, climate change
Analysing the spatial and temporal variability of near-surface air temperature (Ta) is essential for assessing climate change, particularly in polar regions such as the maritime Antarctic, where observational studies remain comparatively scarce. In areas with sparse meteorological networks, satellite observations provide a valuable means of extending station-based analyses and generating spatially distributed Ta maps. This study analyses updated Ta records from six meteorological stations on the Hurd Peninsula, Livingston Island, for 2000–2024, with particular attention to temperature changes since 2016, and evaluates Ta estimation models based on MODIS Terra daytime LST Collection 6.1 data. The analysis of the Ta time series showed significant warming over the complete 2000–2024 period, with trends ranging from 0.53 to 1.27 °C decade−1, and a clear shift towards warming after 2016. While the 2000–2015 period showed spatially contrasting trends, including cooling at JCI, positive trends were observed at all analysed stations during 2016–2024, ranging from 0.40 to 1.33 °C decade−1 and highlighting substantial local variability across the Hurd Peninsula. The global Ta model, developed using data from all six stations and based on MODIS Terra daytime LST and spatiotemporal variables, achieved a performance comparable to that obtained with Collection 6, with R2 = 0.77 and a cross-validated RMSE of 2.23 °C. The results also showed that rigorous filtering of the MODIS LST observations is essential: retaining only good-quality data and excluding observations with |view angle| > 45° substantially reduced dispersion in the Ta–LST relationship and removed unrealistically low LST values. The introduction of this view-angle threshold represents a new filtering step with respect to our previous studies.

item.title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Messori, Hiu-Wang Lau, Chenyu Dong, Gianmarco Mengaldo, Leonardo Olivetti
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, machine learning, extreme event, record-breaking
arXiv:2611.23863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.

item.dc:creator: Ran Chen, Jin-Soo Kim, Jung-Eun Chu, Hyo-Jeong Kim, Bora Lee, Sujong Jeong, … (+1)
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: climate extreme
Mangroves store carbon and protect coasts. We used satellite images and climate models to assess how changing conditions affect mangroves in East Asia. Sunlight and winter temperatures were linked to leaf greenness, sometimes months later. Warming may make northern areas more suitable, but more frequent periods of low sunlight under high emissions could limit these benefits. Conservation and restoration planning should consider both temperature and sunlight, as well as local habitat conditions.

item.title: Uncertainty Estimate for Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature Version 6 (ERSSTv6)
item.dc:creator: Boyin Huang, Xungang Yin, Patrick Hogan, Chunying Liu, Carl J. Schreck, Russell S. Vose, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, proxy, ensemble, neural network
Abstract The NOAA Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature version 6 (ERSSTv6) provides a globally complete monthly SST dataset from 1850 to present, reconstructed from ship, buoy, and near-surface Argo observations using an artificial neural network (ANN) approach. ERSSTv6 incorporates enhanced quality control, large-scale spatial filtering, and an updated ice–SST proxy and includes an operationally feasible and physically consistent uncertainty framework that supports robust assessments of SST variability, trends, and ocean-related applications. We quantify total SST uncertainty as the combination of parametric and reconstruction uncertainties. Parametric uncertainty is estimated from a 1000-member ensemble generated by perturbing 30 internal parameters, including ANN coefficients, quality control, bias adjustments, and ice-SST proxy. ANN-related uncertainty is approximated using a random perturbation (RP) to ANN coefficients, whose magnitude is calibrated by validation errors. Reconstruction uncertainty is assessed with a 500-member ensemble applied to a space-time-complete reference dataset, representing algorithmic error under ideal observations. Results show that grid-scale uncertainty is largest in regions with strong SST variability and sparse data, including western boundary currents, the eastern equatorial Pacific, and ice-covered areas, with global mean uncertainty decreasing from 0.4°–0.5°C in the 1850s to ∼0.3°C after 1950. Uncertainty in global mean SST is smaller, ranging from 0.06°–0.08°C in the 1850s to ∼0.02°C in recent decades. Factor analysis indicates that ANN RP dominates the grid-scale uncertainty, while ship bias correction and ice–SST proxy dominate the uncertainty of global-mean SST. Comparisons show that both SST and its uncertainty in ERSSTv6 are broadly consistent with those other SST products.

item.title: Associations of long-term and short-term summertime temperature with survival among patients with cardiovascular disease: A UK-wide retrospective cohort study
item.dc:creator: Ka Yan Lai, Chris Webster, John Gallacher, Chinmoy Sarkar
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: heat wave
by Ka Yan Lai, Chris Webster, John Gallacher, Chinmoy Sarkar Evidence examining the long-term and acute effects of summertime temperature on survival among patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) is lacking. This study examined associations of both long-term summertime temperature and heatwaves as well as short-term extreme temperature with risk of mortality in patients with CVD and its types. We identified new-onset cases of CVD and its specific types including atrial fibrillation, ischemic heart disease (IHD), heart failure and stroke from linked hospital records in the nationwide UK Biobank cohort. Annual summertime heat exposures in terms of mean temperature and annual heatwaves were measured at 1x1 Km 2 spatial resolution. Daily mean temperature and temperature change between neighbouring days (TCN) were measured over lag 0–5 days. Cox proportional hazard model was used to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs) for long-term associations. We used individual-level time stratified case-crossover design to examine short-term associations of mean daily summertime temperature and TCN with mortality. We identified 63,860 patients with new-onset CVD, of which 12,237 (19.2%) died with mean follow-up of 6.1 years. Each 1°C increment in annual mean summertime temperature was associated with 15% higher risk of mortality for CVD patients (HR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.06-1.24), 10% for atrial fibrillation (1.10; 1.00-1.21), and 19% for IHD (1.19; 1.07-1.33). Risks of mortality remained significantly higher in the group exposed to highest number of annual heatwaves in patients with CVD, and for atrial fibrillation, and heart failure. We identified higher risks of mortality associated with increased summertime temperature in patients of low/moderate (compared with high) education attainment, residing in deprived areas and in neighbourhoods with moderate (compared with high) residential greenspace coverage, suggesting the importance of community planning in climate resilience. Consistently, short-term acute exposure to high temperature was associated with higher risks of mortality for the patient subgroups (OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.23-2.34 for CVD; OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.05-2.42 for atrial fibrillation and OR, 1.67; 95% CI, 1.04-2.67 for IHD). Similarly, positive TCN was associated with higher odds of mortality among patients with CVD, IHD and heart failure as compared with 0 °C temperature change. Our study found that exposure to extreme summertime temperature is a risk factor for mortality among CVD patients. Planning an appropriate mix of community-based strategies together with personalized adaptations for reducing sensitivity to extreme temperature will constitute vital preventive interventions.

item.title: Periglacial Landform Distribution and Rock Glacier Dynamics in a Semiarid Andean Headwater Catchment: Estero Derecho Nature Sanctuary, Chile (~30° S)
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Navarro, Eduardo Yáñez San Francisco, Benjamin Aubrey Robson, Nicole Schaffer, Benjamín Castro-Cancino, Alfonso Fernández, … (+2)
item.description:
Permafrost and Periglacial Processes — matched: glacier
ABSTRACT Rock glaciers are key components of high mountain environments, especially in arid and semiarid regions, where glaciers are scarce. These ice‐debris landforms may act as resilient ice reservoirs and have growing hydrological importance under climate warming. Despite their potential significance, rock glaciers in the semiarid Andes remain understudied, and the climatic controls influencing their distribution and activity are poorly understood. This study examines the topoclimatic controls on the distribution and movement of rock glaciers in the Estero Derecho catchment, a semiarid headwater basin in the Chilean Andes. Detailed inventories of periglacial landforms and, specifically, of rock glaciers were developed following the latest standards of the Rock Glacier Inventory and Kinematics (RGIK) committee. By integrating morphometric, kinematic (using spaceborne Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar), and climatic data, the inventory provides a refined classification of rock glacier activity and offers new insights into their environmental controls. We identified and mapped 60 certain rock glaciers. Most were classified as relict landforms (83%), with only three considered active. Current kinematic activity appears to be controlled by morphometric settings and long‐term thermal conditions, which likely preserve internal structure and ground ice of intact landforms. Notably, at around 4500 m a.s.l., there is a shift towards a lower proportion of movement within intact rock glacier areas and a higher mean annual velocity. Overall, short‐term snow cover variations do not influence activity classification but do modulate seasonal and interannual surface displacement. At El Ternero, the largest rock glacier in the area, peak velocities in late summer correlate with snow cover maxima approximately 7 months earlier. A general trend of deceleration from 2017 to 2024 coincides with rising regional temperatures, a higher 0° isotherm, and declining precipitation during the ongoing Megadrought in Central Chile. These findings highlight the complex interplay between long‐term climate constraints and short‐term snow dynamics in controlling the behavior of rock glaciers under changing climatic conditions.

item.title: Teleconnection processes linking snow cover variability over western Siberia to enhanced early-winter cold waves in South Korea
item.dc:creator: Sangwoo Kim, Eungul Lee
item.description:
The Cryosphere
December cold waves in South Korea have become more frequent over the last 46 years, but their drivers remain unclear. We found that reduced October snow cover in western Siberia increases solar absorption and heat release to the atmosphere. This warming is associated with changes in December circulation, favoring northerly winds that bring cold air into East Asia. October snow cover may serve as one of the precursors for early-winter cold waves, potentially helping reduce socioeconomic impacts.

item.title: Implementation of the reduced complexity model InMAP at urban scale using a high-resolution WRF-Chem simulation
item.dc:creator: Diego Roberto Rojas Neisa, Alejandro Piracoca-Mayorga, Sebastián Espitia-Cano, Ivan Romero-Martinez, Ricardo Morales Betancourt
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
In this work, we explored the ability of simpler atmospheric models to analyze the effectiveness of reducing air pollutant emissions to improve air quality. We showed that, despite its simplicity, these models can be used to estimate the areas where impacts will be felt the most, and therefore, can be used by decision makers to maximize the positive impacts of planned air quality improvements.
